title: Peregrin's Subtle Sparkle
markdown:
Way up where clouds tickle the mountaintops lies the Whispering Peaks Archipelago: jagged crags that tickle the bellies of sky-dwelling cloud-whales, meadows of soft swirling mist like silk scarves, ferry ropes stretched like spiderwebs across breezy chasms that make tummies flip.

On the highest, most ticklish peak, in a cozy tower, lived Peregrin. Not the booming wispy-beard sort. Neat. Exceptionally neat. Cornflower-blue robes pressed, not a thread out. Potion bottles lined by colour, a rainbow in a row. Spells as organised as his sock drawer, which was a marvel. His best friend and most trusted advisor: Noir, a sleek inky-black raven, eyes like polished jet, a caw that could mean the biscuits are ready or the sky is about to fall and looks rather lopsided.

One bright morning, as Peregrin painstakingly polished his favourite crystal ball until it winked like a playful star, Noir landed with an excited flutter. “Caw! Contest!” A bright crinkly flyer at Peregrin’s polished boots.

Never one to be rushed, Peregrin smoothed it. “The annual Village Sparkle Contest. Dazzling displays. Lights like fireflies, music that makes toes tap, fireworks that burst into singing teacups. Quite a spectacle.”

A thoughtful glint. “This year, Noir, I think we shall enter.”

“Caw?” Peregrin usually avoided it. His magic was quiet wonders: morning tea brewing itself, shy flowers in frost. Whispers, not shouts.

“We shall enter,” quiet certainty, “but without trying too hard. A subtle sparkle. Something that shines from the inside.”

The other villagers had begun with the confidence of people who had won before, or believed they ought to. Old Farmer Giles wove a tapestry of captured moonbeams, so shimmering it looked like starlight had sat for a portrait. The Baker twins, flour on their noses, perfected gingerbread fireworks that popped into sweet scent and sugary delight. Mayor Bumblebee planned a parade of hummingbirds dressed as tiny knights, armour gleaming. Everyone assumed bigger, brighter, louder was better. They assumed neatness meant a lack of cleverness.

“They’ll never see it coming,” Peregrin whispered. Noir nodded; the greatest surprises came in quiet packages.

A truly subtle sparkle often needed a rare shimmering dust, grown only high in the echoing caves of Mount Cinder, home of Ignis. A dragon of immense size, scales like a thousand sunsets melting into copper, heart as tender as a butterfly’s wing. He disliked loud noises. He was terribly shy, often feeling overlooked.

They set off, the ferry rope swaying them gently, then rather exhilaratingly, over a dizzying gorge that seemed to drop forever. Noir kept his comments to a single caw that Peregrin translated as hold your hats. When they reached Ignis’s lair the air inside was warm, toasted marshmallows and old comforting books. The dragon was curled in a vast pile, rather glum, mighty tail tucked close, looking overlooked in a cave that could have held a village.

“Greetings, mighty Ignis.” Gentle, respectful. “A small quest. A pinch of your marvelous sparkle-dust, if you please.”

Enormous golden eyes, melted honey. “Sparkle-dust?” A rumble surprisingly soft, pebbles in a warm stream. “Everyone always wants the sparkle. Nobody asks how my day was, or if I enjoyed the cloud-shapes from my perch.” A tiny puff of smoke, a sad smoky sigh.

Peregrin sat, arranging neat robes. Kindness was often the strongest magic. “Your cloud-shapes sound fascinating. I adore cloud-watching. Your scales must catch sunlight in remarkable ways. What was the most interesting cloud today?”

Ignis, surprised and delighted, perked up. Tail thump like a distant drum. He described, with animation, a cloud that looked like a giant fluffy sheep attempting to eat a tiny mischievous mouse, and then, because Peregrin asked, the mouse’s daring escape via a hole that was probably another cloud. Peregrin inquired about the woolly texture and whether the sheep had seemed embarrassed. Ignis had not considered embarrassment in clouds before and found the idea excellent. Noir, on a dripping stalactite, preened with quiet dignity. After a long chat Ignis scooped a generous handful of glittering dust into Peregrin’s pouch, embarrassment replaced by a warm glow on magnificent scales.

“Thank you. Your dust is truly magical. Your cloud-stories were the highlight of my day.”

A soft rumbling purr, a thousand contented cats. “Come back anytime. And bring Noir. He’s a very good listener.”

Back in the tower Peregrin began quiet work. No towering structure, no blazing lights. A single smooth river stone, polished until it gleamed with a soft internal light. The lightest touch, Ignis’s dust. Quiet enchantments: not loudness, but warmth, a gentle steady light that promised comfort.

Contest day arrived with a flurry of excitement and a noisy bustle the tower could hear from the ticklish peak. The village square buzzed. Giles’s tapestry shimmered with heavenly light. Gingerbread fireworks popped little pops of delicious scent, making tummies rumble. Hummingbirds flitted with impressive precision, Mayor Bumblebee buzzing encouragement that was almost a marching tune. Then Peregrin’s turn. He walked to his designated spot and placed the stone on a small unadorned pedestal, as if setting down a cup.

A hush fell over the expectant crowd. “Is that it?” someone muttered, disappointment frank. “Just a plain old rock?”

Peregrin’s neatness, his quiet understated approach, was being mistaken for not much at all. The other displays were blindingly bright, sounds loud and cheerfully celebratory. A familiar pang of doubt began to knot. Perhaps he had misjudged. Perhaps subtle sparkle was not enough, and the sock drawer would have to console him.

“We cannot possibly panic yet,” he said softly to Noir, who watched with sharp intelligent eyes. “We have not even had our afternoon tea, and that is always the first step towards calm contemplation.”

Sun descending, long lazy shadows. A single golden ray, soft as a hug, struck the unassuming stone. It did not burst into a thousand colours or erupt. It absorbed the light, then slowly, gently, began to glow: honey-coloured, a quiet contented joy. The light spread inward, bathing the immediate area in comforting warmth. A captured sunset.

The glow caught a nearby mountain pool; water shimmered like liquid starlight. Villagers who had been dazzled by the boisterous spectacles found themselves drawn. It did not hurt their eyes; it soothed. It did not overwhelm; it invited. The quietest, most profound sparkle.

Mayor Bumblebee, tiny bee-sized monocle gleaming, buzzed over. “Peregrin. This is quite something. Truly.”

One by one they approached, disappointment replaced by hushed awe. They murmured. They saw not a lack of effort but a depth: warmth, comfort, the quiet beauty Ignis had gifted and Peregrin had coaxed.

Noir nudged Peregrin’s cheek, a soft happy caw. He had understood the plan. He had flown to Ignis not only for dust but so Ignis felt seen. That trust had made the difference.

They walked back toward the tower, the stone’s gentle gold lighting the path like a faithful beacon. The contest would be talked about until the next one. The sheep-shaped cloud would be talked about longer, at least in one cave, where Ignis practised describing weather to a stalactite in case Peregrin visited again. Peregrin’s sock drawer, when they got home, was still a marvel. Noir claimed the warmest windowsill. The stone kept a little day after the sun had gone, and afternoon tea, when it came, tasted as if it had been waiting for permission to be calm.
characters: Peregrin (wizard), Noir (raven), Ignis (a mountain dragon with surprisingly delicate feelings)
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing distant-lands fantasy for independent readers
